sources.news_title: Trump Says Russia Will Ship Millions of Tons of Diesel to Bring Down Record Prices
sources.text:
by Simon August
President Donald Trump said Friday that Russia agreed to put millions of tons of diesel on the American and global markets as diesel prices sit near record highs.
Trump wrote in a Truth Social post after a call with Russian President Vladimir Putin that Russia “will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter.”
He said Russia would then deliver another 3 million tons “within a short period of time,” depending on the condition of its refineries.
“Between our TOTAL CONTROL of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian Energy, Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority,” the president added in his post.
“Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority. This is a very big and important announcement. Additionally, it must be understood, that Iran will not have a Nuclear Weapon!” he added.
In response, Volodymyr Zelensky said giving “gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world.”
“Russia will “repay” the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged. What is needed is real de-escalation with Russia on a reciprocal basis,” Zelensky said.
“We count on America’s fair support for our defense of life, for our defense of people in Ukraine – and on the United States having a correspondingly strong conversation with Russia. A strong one, not a weak one,” he added.
U.S. diesel averaged $6.28 a gallon Friday, according to American Automobile Association (AAA) data.
– – –
Simon August is a reporter at Daily Caller News Foundation. Zachery Schmidt is the digital editor of The Star News Network and contributed to this story.

sources.news_title: Trump says US to get diesel from Russia, relaxing pressure on Moscow to ease prices
sources.text:
Trump announces deal with Putin to buy Russian diesel, raising sanctions questions
WASHINGTON (AP) — President Donald Trump said that he has struck a deal to obtain diesel from Russia, a stunning reversal of years of U.S. pressure on Moscow over its war with Ukraine and an attempt to address high fuel prices ahead of the U.S. midterm elections.
Trump said on social media on Friday that he struck the deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin in a phone call in which he was expected to discuss a suspected case of plague in Russia. Instead, Trump announced that Russia will immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by an additional 500,000 tons in November and 1 million tons "immediately thereafter." Russia will deliver another 3 million tons "within a short period of time" after that, he wrote.
Trump's shocking announcement comes after he signed a sweeping Russia sanctions law last month that aimed at clamping down on Russia's energy economy, among other areas, that fuel its war against Ukraine.
His move casts doubt on the likelihood of the White House imposing sanctions on Russia this month, given that a bipartisan law passed by Congress directs the administration to target the top importers of Russian oil and gas.
Trump, in his announcement, did not address the sanctions or Russia's war but said, "Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority."
The White House did not immediately respond to questions about who was paying for the diesel from Russia and when the fuel being supplied under the agreement would become available. It also did not clarify whether subsequent supplies of Russian diesel set to come next month would be supplied prior to Election Day on Nov. 3.
Gas prices globally have surged as the war in Iran upends the energy sector. The national average for a gallon of diesel in the U.S. was $6.23 on Friday, according to AAA, after hitting a record $6.52 on Sept. 22.
Russian presidential envoy Kirill Dmitriev reposted the Treasury Department's announcement on X Friday and said that "Russia-US cooperation on diesel and energy will benefit the world."
Rep. Don Beyer, the senior House Democrat on the Joint Economic Committee, called Trump's announcement "infuriating."
"This is what we warned anyone who would listen: Trump isn't the slightest bit trustworthy when it comes to Russia," Beyer said in a statement on X. "Giving him expanded tariff powers in hopes he would use them to help Ukraine was a mistake. Now he's lifting sanctions on Russian fossil fuels."
The law Trump signed last month envisions sanctions on Russian officials, banks and a shadow fleet of tankers and bans all new U.S. investment in Russia and the handling of sovereign debt.
It also directed Trump to impose tariffs of up to 100% on the top five importers of Russian oil or natural gas, with an exception for countries that import less than 15% of Russia's natural gas exports and have taken significant steps to reduce those imports.
The U.S. has not imported Russian oil or gas since 2022, when the Biden administration banned them because Moscow invaded Ukraine, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration.
Shortly after Trump made the announcement, the Treasury Department said it was immediately issuing a temporary license allowing Russian diesel to be supplied to the global market.
This is the latest in several licenses the U.S. Treasury has issued regarding Russian fuel shipments since the start of the Iran war earlier this year. But it is the first such license to ease sanctions on diesel for a period lasting longer than the standard 30-day window since the start of the Ukraine war.
The new so-called general license means U.S. sanctions will not apply until April 2027 on deliveries of Russian diesel that has been loaded onto tankers as of Friday. The department extended similar easing of sanctions in March and April even though Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent had ruled out such a move earlier in the year.
The extensions continue to underscore how the fallout from the Iran war has boosted Moscow's ability to profit from its energy exports, which had been restrained by the U.S. and other allies since the invasion of Ukraine.

sources.news_title: Trump announces Russia will release millions of tons of diesel to help with skyrocketing costs
sources.text:
Trump announces Russia will release millions of tons of diesel to help with skyrocketing costs
President Trump announced Russia has agreed to provide the world with millions of tons of diesel fuel over the next several months in a bid to decrease skyrocketing global prices.
In a Truth Social post, the president said he had just gotten off the phone with Russian President Vladimir Putin, who had agreed to release 300,000 tons of diesel immediately. He said another 500,000 tons of diesel would be released in November, followed by 1 million tons in December.
"Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel," Mr. Trump continued.
The Treasury Department also announced Friday that it would temporarily waive sanctions on Russia's energy sector to "allow the supply of Russian diesel to the global market."
In a statement from the Kremlin later Friday, Putin confirmed he and Mr. Trump spoke on the phone and that "Russia confirmed its readiness to supply oil and petroleum products to the American and global markets," and he was "confident this will have a positive impact on the entire global economy."
"An agreement was confirmed to continue personal contacts between the presidents of the two countries, as well as cooperation between the presidential administrations, special services, and other agencies," Putin's statement added.
The statement said Putin and Mr. Trump's call touched on "the prospects for resolving the Ukrainian crisis, and the situation surrounding Iran and various aspects of bilateral relations."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy blasted the deal in a social media post, saying any easing of sanctions against Russia is a "weakness."
"Gifts to Putin will not bring peace or any benefit to the civilized world," Zelenskyy said in the post. "Russia will 'repay' the diesel with further terror and perfidy. Allowing Russia to sell petroleum products is an investment in a war that must be ended, not prolonged. What is needed is real de-escalation with Russia on a reciprocal basis."
The moves by the Trump administration mark a reversal of the tight sanctions that have constrained Russia's economy since Putin launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Last month, Mr. Trump signed a bill designed to make it even harder for Russia to profit off oil and gas exports by imposing steep tariffs on the largest buyers of Russian energy.
Mr. Trump had earlier teased a "big announcement coming up on diesel" during remarks Friday at a Columbus Day celebration, but offered little information to speculate on what the announcement would be about.
Mr. Trump pointed out Energy Secretary Chris Wright and said he was "doing a great job."
"We have, I think, some big news on that diesel situation," the president said. "We're gonna be knocking the hell out of it. And remember, what have we done? We stopped Iran from having a nuclear weapon. That's big time. And the prices — the prices will come tumbling."
Diesel prices have skyrocketed in recent months amid the war with Iran. The average price of a gallon of diesel is $6.28, according to AAA, which is up from $5.94 a month ago and $3.68 a year ago.
Diesel had never previously crossed $6 a gallon until just before Labor Day weekend. The record, hit on Sept. 22, was $6.53 per gallon. Diesel is widely used in the trucking, agriculture and construction sectors, so it's a factor for nearly every type of good, including groceries.
The Trump administration has looked into several ways to lower diesel prices, most recently signing an executive order this week allowing the use of red-dyed diesel on highways. Red-dyed diesel is exempt from the federal tax of 24.4 cents a gallon that applies to regular diesel.
The president also argued Thursday that the U.S. has "TOTAL CONTROL" over the Strait of Hormuz, as American forces escort millions of barrels of crude oil through the waterway every night. Iran has continued to target some of those ships, however, including one earlier on Friday.
"Between our TOTAL CONTROL of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian Energy, Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!" Mr. Trump wrote on Truth Social. "Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority. This is a very big and important announcement."

sources.news_title: U.S.-Russia Diesel Deal Goes Beyond Fuel Prices
sources.text:
WASHINGTON, DC – October 10, 2026 (STL.News) U.S.-Russia – Diesel Deal – President Donald Trump‘s announcement of an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin to increase Russian diesel supplies to American and international markets represents more than an effort to reduce fuel prices. The arrangement includes a formal U.S. Treasury sanctions authorization, potentially creates additional commercial opportunities for Russian petroleum exporters, and raises questions about how much relief American businesses and consumers can realistically expect.
Trump announced the agreement Friday, October 9, after a phone call with Putin. The announcement comes as diesel prices remain exceptionally high amid disruptions to international petroleum markets associated with the war involving Iran.
The administration hopes additional Russian diesel will help reduce costs for trucking companies, farmers, manufacturers and other businesses that depend heavily on fuel.
However, energy analysts question whether the proposed supplies will produce sustained price reductions. Much depends on whether the shipments increase worldwide diesel availability or simply redirect existing supplies from one group of customers to another.
The most significant confirmed development is the Treasury Department’s issuance of a temporary authorization covering specified Russian diesel transactions. It remains uncertain whether the announced quantities will be delivered and whether they will materially reduce American fuel prices.
U.S.-Russia Diesel Deal – Trump Announces Russian Diesel Supply Commitments
Trump said Russia had agreed to make more than 300,000 metric tons of diesel available immediately to American and international markets.
According to his October 9 announcement, Russia would provide another 500,000 metric tons in November, followed by an additional 1 million metric tons shortly afterward.
Trump also described a further 3 million metric tons that Russia could supply within a relatively short period, depending on the operating condition of its refineries.
If all those amounts represent separate supplies and are fulfilled, the announced total would exceed 4.8 million metric tons.
However, those figures reflect quantities Trump announced rather than independently verified completed deliveries.
The public announcement did not establish that American purchasers had contracted, shipped, or received the full amounts.
It also did not specify how much diesel would be delivered directly to the United States rather than sold to international buyers.
Those distinctions matter because fuel promised to international markets does not necessarily become additional fuel available to American businesses.
The economic effect will depend on actual shipments, their destinations, and whether they improve supply conditions in markets experiencing shortages.
U.S.-Russia Diesel Deal – Treasury Issues Russian Diesel Authorization
The agreement involves a concrete regulatory action by the U.S. Treasury Department.
On October 9, the Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control issued Russia-related General License 135, titled “Authorizing Transactions Related to the Sale, Delivery, Offloading, and Importation of Diesel Fuel of Russian Federation Origin.”
The license authorizes specified transactions involving Russian-origin diesel under the sanctions regulations identified in the document.
The authorization covers qualifying activities involving the sale, delivery, offloading, and importation of Russian diesel. It remains effective until April 7, 2027.
However, General License 135 does not comprehensively remove U.S. sanctions against Russia.
A Treasury general license permits specified activities that would otherwise be prohibited under the sanctions programs it covers, provided those transactions satisfy the license’s conditions.
The authorization must also be distinguished from separate federal laws governing Russian energy imports.
Congress enacted the Ending Importation of Russian Oil Act in April 2022, establishing a statutory prohibition on imports of specified Russian energy products.
General License 135 and that statute are separate legal authorities.
The issuance of the Treasury license does not, by itself, establish that the statutory prohibition has been terminated or that every proposed direct shipment into the United States has satisfied all applicable legal requirements.
That distinction is important because the administration’s announcement concerns both American and international markets.
The Treasury authorization changes how qualifying Russian diesel transactions are treated under specified sanctions regulations without showing that every proposed physical import has been legally cleared.
The regulatory action nevertheless makes the arrangement more than a diplomatic announcement.
U.S.-Russia Diesel Deal – Diesel Prices Put Pressure on American Businesses
The administration’s main economic objective is to ease the financial pressure from high diesel prices.
According to AAA figures reported by The Associated Press, the national average diesel price was about $6.28 per gallon on October 9.
That compared with approximately $3.68 per gallon a year earlier, an increase of about 71%.
Diesel is essential to American freight transportation, agriculture, construction and industrial production.
Commercial trucks transport groceries, manufactured products, building materials, and consumer goods nationwide.
Agricultural producers depend on diesel-powered tractors, harvesting machinery and transportation vehicles.
Construction contractors use diesel in heavy equipment, while railroads and industrial operators rely on distillate fuels for important operations.
When diesel prices rise, transportation and production expenses often increase.
Those costs can eventually affect consumers through higher shipping charges and prices for food, merchandise, and services.
For companies operating large commercial fleets, even relatively small changes in fuel prices can substantially affect profitability.
Reducing diesel costs is therefore an important economic objective with consequences extending throughout the American economy.
However, announcing additional fuel supplies does not guarantee lower prices.
U.S.-Russia Diesel Deal – Will Russian Diesel Actually Lower American Prices?
The proposed Russian supplies must be weighed against American and global fuel demand.
The initial 300,000 metric tons represents approximately 2.2 million barrels of diesel, depending on the fuel’s density.
That is less than one day of total U.S. distillate fuel consumption.
The larger announced quantities could provide more substantial supplies if delivered, but the agreement concerns American and international markets rather than exclusively the United States.
Energy analysts interviewed by The Associated Press questioned whether the arrangement would significantly reduce diesel prices.
Their concern centers on the difference between increasing worldwide supply and redirecting existing shipments.
If Russian diesel is diverted from established customers to American buyers, those customers may need to obtain replacement supplies from other exporters.
In that situation, the agreement could change international trading patterns without materially increasing worldwide diesel production.
Additional shipments might still improve availability in particular regions.
However, localized improvements would not necessarily produce a sustained nationwide decline in American diesel prices.
The distinction between additional production and redistribution of existing supplies is central to understanding the agreement’s potential economic impact.
U.S.-Russia Diesel Deal – Analysts Question the Scale of the Benefits
Energy specialists cited by The Associated Press expressed skepticism that the proposed Russian deliveries would significantly reduce American diesel prices.
Their analysis reflects a basic limitation in global petroleum markets.
A country can increase exports to one destination without increasing its total production.
If existing customers must obtain replacement fuel elsewhere, the effect on worldwide prices may be modest.
The agreement could therefore improve regional availability without producing broad price reductions.
Russia could also benefit commercially from additional export opportunities, although revenue would depend on completed sales and their terms.
The public announcements do not establish the total value of those transactions.
Consequently, the agreement’s potential benefits for Russian producers should be distinguished from any measurable savings for American consumers.
U.S.-Russia Diesel Deal – Diesel Markets React to Trump’s Announcement
Financial markets responded quickly to the news.
Contemporary market reporting described a decline in U.S. diesel futures following Trump’s announcement.
The move reflected expectations that additional Russian fuel could ease supply pressure.
However, changes in futures prices should not be confused with actual savings for American businesses.
Retail diesel prices depend on crude oil costs, refinery operations, transportation expenses, inventories, taxes, and regional demand.
A short-term decline in futures prices does not establish that Russian diesel has reached American buyers.
It also does not guarantee that retail prices will remain lower.
If expected shipments are delayed or broader supply conditions deteriorate, initial market optimism could fade.
For American truckers, farmers and manufacturers, the more important measure will be sustained changes in the prices they actually pay.
U.S.-Russia Diesel Deal – Global Energy Disruptions Complicate the Outlook
The agreement comes amid significant disruptions to international petroleum markets associated with the conflict involving Iran.
The Middle East plays a major role in global crude oil production, refining and petroleum transportation.
The Strait of Hormuz is particularly important because substantial volumes of international energy shipments pass through the waterway.
Disruptions involving petroleum production, refining, or shipping can affect fuel availability far beyond the region.
Diesel supply depends not only on crude oil production but also on refineries’ capacity to produce finished petroleum products.
Even when crude oil is available, limited refining capacity can constrain diesel output and contribute to higher prices.
Additional Russian diesel could help offset some shortages, but it cannot automatically replace all the refining capacity or transportation flows affected by broader international disruptions.
Global prices will continue to depend on refinery operations, shipping conditions, inventories, and demand.
Those factors could limit the agreement’s effectiveness even if Russia fulfills its announced commitments.
U.S.-Russia Diesel Deal – Russian Refinery Problems Raise Delivery Questions
Russia’s ability to supply the proposed quantities remains another important uncertainty.
Ukraine has repeatedly targeted Russian petroleum refineries and related energy infrastructure during the war.
Those attacks have disrupted refining operations and complicated Russia’s ability to meet domestic fuel demand while maintaining exports.
Russia has also restricted diesel exports to protect domestic availability.
These conditions raise questions about whether Moscow can fulfill the proposed delivery schedule without creating additional pressure on its own fuel market.
Removing export restrictions would not automatically restore damaged refining capacity.
Russian producers must still produce enough diesel, meet domestic demand, and arrange transport to international buyers.
Seasonal changes in fuel demand could also affect how much diesel is available for export.
Trump’s announcement explicitly linked the possibility of larger additional supplies to the condition of Russian refineries.
That qualification matters because the largest proposed quantities depend on production capabilities that remain vulnerable to disruption.
The agreement could create opportunities for additional Russian exports without guaranteeing that all announced shipments will occur.
U.S.-Russia Diesel Deal – Russia Could Benefit From Additional Energy Sales
For Russia, the arrangement offers potential commercial advantages.
Russia remains a major producer and exporter of petroleum products, but sanctions and wartime disruptions have complicated its international energy business.
The Treasury authorization creates additional opportunities for qualifying transactions involving Russian diesel.
Completed sales could generate revenue for Russian petroleum producers and exporters.
However, the announcement alone does not establish the amount of additional revenue.
The public information does not identify all buyers, contract prices, payment arrangements, or completed shipment volumes.
Therefore, it would be premature to assign a specific financial value to the proposed agreement.
Russia could benefit from expanded export opportunities even if American diesel prices experience only modest relief.
The arrangement also has broader international implications because restrictions on Russian energy revenue have been part of the economic measures imposed following Moscow’s invasion of Ukraine.
Those considerations do not determine whether the agreement will benefit American businesses, but they help explain its overall significance.
U.S.-Russia Diesel Deal – What American Truckers and Farmers Should Watch
For American businesses, the agreement’s practical value will ultimately depend on fuel availability and prices.
Trucking companies could benefit if additional diesel supplies reduce wholesale costs and improve regional inventories.
Farmers could experience similar benefits during fuel-intensive planting, harvesting, and transportation operations.
Construction companies, manufacturers and distributors could also benefit from lower transportation and equipment expenses.
However, the announcement does not establish that diesel prices will decline by a specific amount or that additional supplies will reach every American region.
Businesses should distinguish between announced supply commitments, confirmed commercial shipments, and actual changes in fuel costs.
Important indicators include Russian diesel export volumes, U.S. distillate inventories, refinery production, wholesale diesel prices, and regional retail price trends.
Those measures will provide a clearer assessment of the agreement’s effectiveness than announced quantities alone.
The arrangement could help stabilize the market without resolving broader global supply disruptions.
Its practical value will become clearer as shipment and pricing information becomes available.
U.S.-Russia Diesel Deal – Why the U.S.-Russia Diesel Deal Is More Than Symbolic
The agreement has two distinct dimensions.
The first is economic. Additional Russian diesel could improve fuel availability during a period of elevated prices and international supply disruptions.
The second is regulatory and commercial. The Treasury Department has issued a formal authorization covering specified transactions involving Russian-origin diesel.
That action represents a real change in the administration of U.S. sanctions.
However, several important questions remain unanswered.
Publicly available information does not show that all announced quantities have been contracted or delivered.
It does not establish how much diesel will reach American buyers, what prices purchasers will pay, or whether shipments will produce sustained retail savings.
Separate statutory restrictions governing Russian energy imports also mean the Treasury authorization should not be interpreted as automatically resolving every legal issue associated with direct U.S. imports.
For American businesses, the decisive issue will be whether the arrangement produces measurable improvements in fuel availability and costs.
For Russian producers, the potential benefit lies in additional export opportunities and commercial revenue.
For international energy markets, the arrangement could alter trade flows and ease selected shortages without necessarily increasing total worldwide production.
The U.S.-Russia diesel agreement is more than symbolic because it includes a Treasury sanctions authorization and proposed commercial supplies. Whether it effectively responds to America’s diesel price problem remains unproven. The ultimate test will be completed shipments, additional fuel availability, and sustained reductions in diesel costs.

sources.news_title: Trump Announces Russia Deal To Supply Diesel To US
sources.text:
Trump Announces Russia Deal To Supply Diesel To US
United States President Donald Trump has announced an agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin for Russia to supply millions of tons of diesel fuel to the US and global markets.
Trump disclosed the agreement in a post on his Truth Social platform on Friday, saying Russia would immediately release more than 300,000 tons of diesel, followed by additional shipments in the coming months.
He said Russia would supply another 500,000 tons in November, followed by one million tons shortly afterwards.
Trump added that Russia would deliver a further three million tons within a short period, depending on the condition of its diesel refineries.
The US president said the additional supplies would help reduce fuel prices, particularly for American farmers, ranchers and truckers.
“Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST!” he wrote.
Trump also linked the proposed supplies to the ongoing disruption around the Strait of Hormuz, claiming that the United States had “TOTAL CONTROL” of the strategic waterway.
He reiterated that Iran would not be allowed to acquire a nuclear weapon, without providing further details of his discussion with Putin on the issue.
Following Trump’s announcement, the US Treasury Department said its Office of Foreign Assets Control would issue a temporary general licence permitting Russian diesel supplies to the global market, easing restrictions that have limited Russia’s energy trade.
The announcement comes as fuel prices have risen amid the war involving the United States, Israel and Iran, which has disrupted energy supplies and shipping through the Strait of Hormuz.
Diesel is widely used in freight transport, agriculture and other industries, making its price a significant factor in the cost of moving goods.
The proposed arrangement also marks a shift in Washington’s approach to Russian energy exports, following years of sanctions imposed over Moscow’s war against Ukraine.

sources.news_title: Trump Reopens to Russian Diesel Through 2027 in Agreement with Putin
sources.text:
President Donald Trump extraordinarily announced that he has reached an agreement with Russian leader Vladimir Putin to import Russian diesel through spring 2027 and keep fuel prices in the United States in check. The decision came after a phone call between the two heads of state, while special envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff are in Miami this weekend for a high-level summit with delegations from Ukraine, France, Germany, the European Union, and NATO.
No details are available regarding the terms of the agreement—including payment or any reciprocal concessions—except for the supply volumes: an initial shipment of 300,000 metric tons will arrive, followed by additional deliveries in the coming months, until the total reaches three million metric tons. These are modest quantities: 300,000 metric tons amount to less than one day’s worth of U.S. diesel consumption.
The Treasury has suspended sanctions on Russian diesel until April 7, 2027.
The United States had not imported Russian energy since February 2022, when Russia invaded Ukraine, and the decision—made against the backdrop of an election campaign in which Trump’s approval ratings are at historic lows in the polls due to rising fuel prices—has drawn sharp criticism.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy called the decision “unworthy” and “weak,” arguing that revenue from energy exports will allow the Kremlin to prolong the conflict. Several Democratic members of Congress have also accused Trump of betraying Kyiv and European allies, putting U.S. national security at risk. The agreement is a financial lifeline for the Russian war machine, as former U.S. Ambassador to Moscow McFaul put it: “Not only has he cut military aid to Ukraine, but now he’s giving Putin new money to build more missiles and drones.”
Trump ended the call with a resounding: “Thank you, Putin.”
